en.justification: Caravaggio depicted the key moment in the Old Testament story of David and his victory over the giant Goliath. It has already been recognised that Goliath's face is a self-portrait of the artist, but there is an opinion that David is a self-portrait as well, representing the artist as a young man.

At the early stage of his career Annibale Carracci was strongly influenced by Venetian painters, especially Tintoretto, but the figures of the Apostles in this painting derive from Raphael's *Transfiguration* in the Pinacoteca Vaticana.

The biblical theme celebrates the virtue of chastity. The canvas, a replica of the fresco in Palazzo Mattei in Rome, is a play on light with a clearly theatrical inspiration. The diagonal of Joseph’s gesture lends additional dynamic to the overall movement of the composition.
The painting was made during Rubens’s first stay in Rome (1602). He matched Barocci's colours, the dense brushwork of late Titian, Roman statuary and the light and shadow of Caravaggio.
The monochrome colour scheme, light contrasts and the artist’s original handwriting hint at inspiration from Dutch 17th-century painting.

The painting is one of four works by Benković who was commissioned by Count Franz Lothar von Schönborn, elector and Archbishop of Mainz and Prince Bishop of Bamberg in 1715, while he was refurbishing the family castle in Pommersfelden.

Lanfranco's masterpiece *Assumption of the Virgin* was inspired by Correggio's Proto-Baroque dome-fresco depicting the same theme, which was executed between 1526 and 1530 in Parma Cathedral. The vortex of figures is unique in the art of 17th-century Rome.
Painted on the flat ceiling, Pozzo’s *quadratura* extends real architectural space into open sky, where the apotheosis of St. Ignatius takes the central role.

Although not very well known to the public, it is a fundamental example of Bolognese prospective *quadratura*. Painted illusionistic architecture displays columns and pillars which stand on false parapets or balustrades. The *trompe l'oeil* effect is extremely convincing and gives the impression of resting on a genuine plaster cornice.

“Real” architecture in the central representational space of the abbey is supplemented by illusionary painting, with the subject of Christ at a Common Table culminating in the figure of Divine Providence with a cornucopia.

The Church of St. George is not the only completely painted Baroque church in Croatia, but it shows by far one of the most consistent concepts of painted architecture and decorative elements, an excellent example of *quadratura*, which visually expands the modest one-nave space of the church.
Ranger relied a great deal on Pozzo’s *Perspectiva pictorum et architectorum*, but there is no exact parallel to this illusionistic dome in Pozzo’s book.

The illusionist balcony opens just above the apse, where on the eastern wall, the battle between the saint and the dragon is taking place. The scene brings to mind almost voyeuristically the scene in the Cornaro Chapel in Rome.

Only by walking through the perspective do we realise the deceptive optical effect produced by Borromini: the mosaic floor is placed on a slope, so as one proceeds towards the end part of the vault it is lower, and the distance between the columns is reduced both in depth and in width.
The terracotta was modelled by Bernini in Rome for an equestrian monument of Louis XIV, but the sculpture itself was executed by his pupils.
The drawing, one of only a few of its kind to survive, refers to the decoration of the bridge in Náměšť nad Oslavou. Josef Winterhalder came from a family of sculptors in Schwarzwald.

A cabinet with the appearance of an architectural façade fitted with drawers for valuables. Richly decorated with painted glass panels framed with ebony and tortoiseshell, it stands on its own luxuriously carved and gilt base.
The decorative repertoire of the glass compositions consist of figures, mythological scenes and views treated in the antique manner.
The painted scenes are in the style of the Baroque painter Luca Giordano.

The extraordinary vivacity of this mirror frame testifies at a very early stage (1699) to the great skill and the refined taste of Bolognese Baroque carvers who looked to Rome and Venice for up-to-date ideas.
The base of the console comprises vine-shoots and grapes naturalistically intertwined using emphatically realistic carving.

Decorated in the Rococo style with French and Italian influences, the coach has a closed body with elegant curving lines and glazed windows. It is lined with red velvet and the rear wheels are decorated with the 12 signs of the zodiac.

A symbol of the early Counter-Reformation in Bologna (more appropriately of the Catholic Reformation) for its authentic and direct religious feeling. It is one of several paintings from Lombardy and northern Italy that is seen as leading up to the style of Caravaggio thanks to its humble naturalism and its original experiments with light.

The painting was commissioned by the Confraternity of the Papal Grooms for the Sant’Anna Chapel located in Saint Peter’s Basilica. The religious theme is handled in an innovative and powerfully humanised way. Caravaggio’s use of light greatly influenced his contemporaries, even the more classical painters.

Manuel Pereira built unique Iberian Baroque sculptural figures. This powerful Christ figure, inspired by an engraving of Pontius Pilate from a composition by Rubens, shows a theatrical expression and a dynamic force on his lifeless body.

The Crucified Christ is at the centre of the painting; the Holy Father hovers in the clouds holding up the cross, supported in the lower part by two angels. Above His head the Holy Ghost – a dove radiating light – is surrounded by cherubs.

The painting, which depicts the revelation of the Apostle Thomas who doubted Christ’s resurrection, is enhanced by the sculpted component of St. Augustine with a burning heart, which becomes almost part of the miraculous scene.
Borromini's work on Sant’Ivo was a long-term undertaking: the building structure was erected in 1650 but the decorative elements were not complete until 1660 under Pope Alexander VII.

To the concave façade Borromini opposed the convexity of the dome drum consisting of a low stepped pyramid, whose strong pressure to the outside is plastically defined by pilasters overlapping the corners.
The lantern with its twin columns repeats the pattern of centrifugal forces and resolves the innovative invention of the spiral crowning culminating in an iron crown, an orb and a cross.
The façade is one of the most perfect examples of Baroque theatricality applied to urban planning: a semi-circular portico links up with the sides, like two theatrical wings.
The church, with some new ideas, bears a typical Counter-Reformation plan, referencing the Roman Jesuit church of the Gesù.

The Pilgrimage Church of the Premonstratensian Abbey Steingaden was created by Dominikus Zimmermann with support of his brother, Johann Baptist. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage Site list in 1983.

The expansive intertwining shapes and movement of light provide striking dynamism. Here, V. Vejmluva established a “spiritual mausoleum” for John of Nepomuk, a saint canonised in 1729, and whose cult became one of the most widespread in Central Europe.

The most representative Croatian church with an oval plan located in the manor of the Zagreb diocese in Sela kod Siska. The special value of this Late Baroque church with characteristic features of the Rococo style is evident in the shaping of the convex façade flanked by two bell towers with concave sides.

Cardinal Borghese commissioned Bernini to sculpt the David when he was 25 years old. The artist had the intuition to stop the biblical hero just one second before the shot, placing Goliath in the viewer's space.
Algardi’s interpretation of the free-standing group is greatly influenced by Andrea Sacchi’s (1559–1661) *Martyrdom of St Longinus at Castelgandolfo*.

Frei Cipriano da Cruz is one of the most extraordinary Portuguese monk-sculptors and one of the best representatives of the country’s Baroque sculpture. Based on models that circulated throughout Europe, the *Pietà* is one of his best achievements. The theme meets the most essential Tridentine ideals. It is part of an ensemble of pieces made for St. Bento Church, the church of his Order’s college in Coimbra, which was demolished in 1932.
The dramatic scene of treason from the Gospel of St. Matthew exemplifies the typical Baroque motif of expressive motion.

The Altar of the Holy Cross is the final and most mature achievement of the sculptor Franceso Robba who, through his artistic achievements, is a notable figure in European Baroque sculpture and altar-making.

Georg Raphael Donner, one of the most prominent Central European sculptors of the first-half of the 18th century, developed his individual Neoclassical style at a distance from the Baroque tradition, relying on models from antiquity and 16th-century Italian sculpture. The adoring angels belong to the very peak of his oeuvre.

Gian Lorenzo Bernini executed the group between 1622 and 1625. Such a pagan myth (Ovid, *Metamorphosis*) in the cardinal's house is explained by a moral distich by Maffeo Barberini (Urbano VIII, 1623–44) on the theme of Vanitas: “those who love to pursue fleeting forms of pleasure, in the end find only leaves and bitter berries in their hands.”

The funerary monuments combine the solemn symmetry of the triangularly shaped upright "sarcophagus" standing on the lion's paws and vividly animated figures of angels, one writing the epitaph on Antonio Barberini’s tomb and the other playing the trumpet on the tomb of Taddeo Barberini.

Alessandro Algardi (b. 1595, Bologna–d. 1654, Rome) made this statue for the library of the Convent of St. Michael near Bologna, and it dates to the last period of his activity. The struggle between the archangel and the devil compelled the artist to abandon his usual controlled style and adopt a more complex and violent rhythm, while still looking for the ideal both in elegance and beauty.
The visual effect of the sculpture is enhanced by the treatment of its surfaces: gold plate combined with matt and gloss finishes.
Schweigl ornamented the soft surface of the statue with folds and incisions in the hem of the cloak.
The soulful face corresponds with traditional representations of St. John the Evangelist, his fine facial features off-set with locks of wavy hair.

The entire altar as well as the decorative drapery, which in places grows into abstractly dramatic labyrinths hiding the body of the saint, is monochrome, and gives the illusion that it is carved in marble.

A closer look at the detail shows differentiated surfaces as if to stress the illusion of different structures. With his eyes closed and his head leaning against his right shoulder, the saint is in deep meditation.

The gold-plated surfaces tenderly reflect light and produce the soft, shimmering effect of the whole. The expressive gestures of the Old Testament prophets and their interaction with the space around and into which they merge with their bodies reveal characteristics of quality Baroque sculptures.
The most dramatic scene is seen on the canopy: God the Father handing Moses the Tablets of the Law, Aaron, on the left shown as a bishop, and Joshua, on the right, dressed in military clothes.
The return of Joshua and Caleb who went as spies to Canaan. The almost dancing movements suggest the frivolous nature of the Rococo.

The gold-thread relief embroidery of the Holy Sepulchre covers eight panels and contains 16 oval medallions, which bordered by gold cartouches, contain scenes from the Old and New Testaments.  
  
The Bishop of Zagreb, Petar Petretić, commissioned the Sepulchre from the German embroiderer, Wolfgang Jakob Stoll.

The antependium with scenes from the legends of St. Joseph is one of only a few examples of the use of figurative embroidery in sacred art during the first-half of the 18th century, and a specimen of monastery art.

The red background of the chasuble is divided into fields by silver lace. Two garlands of leaves unfurl against a net ground, the sides of which are marked with a dangling garland motif also against a net ground. The central pole springs from an acanthus bush with the instruments of the Passion of Christ in its spires.

This vessel, for carrying the embodiment of Christ's flesh, the Host, is one of only a few gold monstrances in Europe. The typically Baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation encircles a case with a lunette, the crescent for holding the Host. The sunburst symbolises the source of life, light and Divine truth.

Holding the solar sphere made out of silver – glowing with the true Word of God – the Atlantes angel is supposed to increase the emotional and devotional fervour of the congregation and lead them to contemplate the Divine light of truth and its beauty.

Commissioned by King D. Pedro II, this Reliquary Chest is engraved in low-relief with scenes of St. João de Brito’s life and martyrdom. The bas-relief on the top features the saint in Indian dress, wearing sandals and carrying a staff.

The canvas was painted for Cardinal Pietro Aldobrandini, nephew of the preceding Pope Clement VIII, who had a strong dislike for the Borghese family. However, Cardinal Scipione wanted the painting for himself and had it forcibly removed from the artist's studio, imprisoning the artist for several days.

The painting is part of a series depicting the Four Seasons painted for the counts Legnani by Pier Francesco Cittadini, a Milanese painter celebrated for his still-lives and portraits. Bacchus, supervising the wine-making, personifies the allegory of Autumn; a wreath of seasonal fruit, following the Flemish tradition, frames the scene.
The painting is an admirable *veduta*, showing two outstanding building projects carried out during the reign of King D. Manuel (1495–1521): the Belém Tower and the Jerónimos Monastery.

The decorative composition of a pair of nudes in dramatic poses conveys a story from Greek mythology retold by Ovid in the third volume of *Metamorphoses*. The painted frame of the picture suggests that the canvas was part of an interior decoration, the location for which is as yet unknown.

Bogdány was a Hungarian painter who studied in Vienna and in Amsterdam where sources mention him in 1684, and where he may have pursued his studies. Amsterdam, then the centre of middle-class genres, especially still-life, was a perfect school for an artist just starting out.

The marble bust is by the Roman sculptor of French origin Pierre-Etienne Monnot. Prince Livio Odescalchi was a member of the influential Italian family known historically to have produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI.

The most significant architectural work carried out involved the gardens, which – along with the long wing of the building (*manica*) – make up a single group comprising different structures, including a water theatre or *nymphaeum* opposite the portico of the secret garden, which were built alongside the new Borghese wings.

The monumental and sumptuous villa of the noble Albergati family stands in the fertile countryside around Bologna and can be considered one of the most significant examples of Italian 17th-century residential architecture.

The chateau, outbuildings and park, once the seat of the most powerful aristocratic family in Moravia, make up the monument which is listed on the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site list. The count’s residence, which was the satellite for culture, was also the centre for economic administration for a large demesne in Valtice.

A summer palace belonging to the Portuguese court which developed around a former palace. From the outside, the main façade forms a semi-circular plan around a Neoclassical statue of Queen Maria I by Joaquim José Aguiar. The interior has a U-shaped floor-plan embracing a “French-style” garden, with other wings bordering the park.

The Esterházy Palace complex in Fertőd-Eszterháza is an outstanding creation of 18th-century European and Hungarian palace architecture; a *maison de' plaisance* – “merry residence”, or *Lustschloss* in German – that was constantly reshaped, along with its garden, by its Maecenas, Nikolaus Esterházy, from the 1750s to the 1780s.

*Maison de plaisance* in the French Late Regency style, built for the Bavarian prince elector’s wife Maria Amalia of Habsburg. The design is by François Cuvilliés and the execution of the fine stuccoes are by Johann Baptist Zimmermann.

The wooden relief shows features typical of Early Baroque sculpture from Bavaria: it is still strongly connected to the Late Mannerist style and characteristic of early 17th-century Northern and Central European sculpture.
Komerseiner’s statues illustrate a new style expressed in the mobility of the slender figures of saints in characteristic counterpoise, freeing them from dependence on altarpiece niches.

The arrival of the sculptor Komersteiner to Zagreb marked the final entrance of Baroque sculpture to continental Croatia. Komersteiner introduced the Baroque acanthus as a decorative element and was Northwest Croatia’s most important sculptor at the turn of the Baroque centuries.
The statues were promoted into the vanguard of Rococo sculpture in Hungary by the outstanding quality of modelling, the subtle and reserved colouring and the empathic rendering of emotions.
St. Sebastian and St. Roch, who were both patron saints against the plague, are typical of the style of one of Styria’s most important Baroque sculptors.

Bartolomeo’s painting was made for the High Altar of St. Michael's Church in Sopron. The pompous composition shows similarities to Francesco Solimena's (d. 1747) most popular work, the fresco in San Domenico Maggiore in Naples of 1709.
The artist’s virtuoso brushwork and use of light are characteristic of the original style of Maulbertsch, a prominent artist of the Habsburg monarchy in the 18th century.
The drama of the moment is underlined by visible impasto, underlined by intense accents of light.
The expressive surface of the painting is typical of Maulbertsch’s pictorial style.

Lusitano was influenced by Roman, Late Baroque and Rococo art; his teachers included Benedetto Lutti (1666–1724) and Francesco Trevisani (1656–1746), a disciple of Carlo Maratta (1625–1713). The pompous composition clearly shows the influence of a Roman academic training.

A shortage of economic resources prompted Andrea Pozzo to create an illusory extension to the church by painting a prolongation of the choir behind the high altar, which contains a mock shrine, and stands before a representation of the Circumcision of Jesus.

Both the construction and the interior decoration of the monumental church (53.5 m x 12.5 m x 24.5 m) were largely executed by local builders and artists. It was based on a traditional model, exemplified by the Jesuit church Il Gesú, in Rome.

The interior of the church is a unique work of art created by the Asam brothers as their own private church. Architecture, sculpture, ceiling-painting and furniture complement each other to achieve an exceptional visual impression.

The Pilgrimage and Parish Church of Our Lady of the Snow in Belec, a votive church for which the donors were prominent members of Croatian nobility, was completely equipped in the fourth decade of the 18th century with an inventory of superior value: a luxurious main altar, extraordinary side altars, the pulpit, the choir railing and the ceiling-painting represent high quality *Gesamtkunstwerk* (lit. total work of art).
The interior of the church is decorated with frescoes and stuccowork in the tradition of the so-called Wessobrunner School.

The Jesuit Church and Monastery of Székesfehérvár, built between 1745 and 1756, is a marvellous example of a unified whole created by various artists in a relatively small period of time, crowned by Sambach’s elaborate illusionist painting.

The intentional simplicity of the façade, punctuated by pilaster strips and the papal coat-of-arms and characterised by a high, ribbed cupola, contrasts with the elegance of the interior – a Greek cross – where Raggi’s rich and detailed decorative stuccowork in white and gold covers the high altar.

The playful composition of massive stucco decoration dominates the small space of the chapel. Although the formal vocabulary of ornament is characteristic of Late Mannerism, its impact on the viewer is closer to the intentions of the Baroque.
*St Michael defeating the Devil* is made of stucco and stands over the main door, in the counter-façade.
Allegorical figures of Mercy, Charity, Justice, Humility, Penitence, and Wisdom are moulded in stucco and placed between side-chapels of the church.
Figures are placed between Corinthian columns, above wooden confessional boxes.

Cobalt-blue tiles cover the interior walls, ceiling and cupola, submerging the visitor in their ambiance immediately on entering the church. They show the European taste in Chinese porcelain at the time.
The subject of the tile painting is the Life, Death and Coronation of St. Laurence. Born in Spain, St. Laurence was a martyr in Rome.
Glazed, painted tiles (*azulejos*), in cobalt-blue and gold on a white background. The tiles, which form the bust of the person and superior part of the halberd, show special carved contours.
To enhance the *trompe l'’oeil* illusion, the halberdiers are drawn to natural scale, as if they were actors on the set of an opera.

The remarkable blue-and-white tile composition, by an artist from the workshop circle of Oliveira Bernardes, reveals a sophisticated technique and an artistic capacity to transform these moralising figurative *azulejos* into impressive iconographic themes.
The column, crowned by the Virgin Mary vanquisher of evil, was erected in gratitude at the end of the plague epidemic. It was among the first columns of its kind in Moravia.
On the top of the column there is a sculpture of the Immaculate Virgin with stars around her head.

The Holy Trinity column in Sopron, with its pedestal decorated with figures of saints and patrons, is one of Hungary’s most beautiful Baroque monuments. Erected between 1697 and 1701 to commemorate the end of the plague epidemic, it was built in the sentiment of both plight and gratitude.
Standing on the ledges of the mid-level pedestal-columns are ancillary figures of St. James, St. Stephen King of Hungary and, at the corners, St. John of Nepomuk and St. Anthony of Padua.

A votive monument to commemorate liberation from Bavarian troops in 1703. A statue of the Immaculate Virgin stands atop the Corinthian pillar; at the base are sculptures of St. Anne, St. George, St. Vigil and St. Cassian.
The statues, which are made in the tradition of Bernini, are reminiscent of the High Baroque.

The Holy Trinity Column, Buda, built between 1710 and 1714, stood in front of the Parish Church of the Holy Virgin and the Old Town House of Buda. During World War I in 1916, the column was the scene of the coronation of King Charles IV Habsburg. It was demolished at the end of the 19th century.

The column celebrates the Church and the Christian tradition of the city. The sculpture atop the column is of Christ the Saviour and God the Father as the ruler of the world. This opens out to the Archangel Michael, the symbol of the eternal struggle with heresy. The work, by several Olomouc masters, is one of the last memorial columns to be built in several towns from the second-half of the 17th century onwards, under the Habsburg monarchy.

The importance of the motif of the dove of the Holy Spirit on a sunburst is eminently underlined by the rays of the rising sun. Even the Augsburg masters took an interest in the gilding of the copper statues.

On a high pedestal with strong volutes and inscription cartouches a tall column ascends which is crowned by the Holy Trinity enthroned on picturesque clouds from which protrude numerous angelic heads.
At the foot of the column stand the protectors from the plague, St. Charles Borromeo, St. Francis Xavier, St. Roch and St. Sebastian, while St. Rosalia lies on her stone bed.

The Spanish Steps were built to link piazza di Spagna with Via Felice, the first great street planned by Pope Sixtus V (1585). Several other projects by Alessandro Specchi were realised between 1717 and 1720.

Passalacqua inventively reinterpreted the Roman town-plan for use in Dubrovnik. With a convex–concave, axially conceived staircase space (in the axis of which is the entrance to the college) he created a deep scenic vista, with which in a distinctive Late Baroque manner, he integrated the Jesuit complex into the structure of the city.

The square is an example of the modern-age urban concept; an effort to create a compact whole. The unique complex of Renaissance and Baroque houses has been listed as part of the UNESCO World Cultural Heritage Site list.
The square is lined with picturesque houses with gables and arcades closed-off by the chateau to the west.
Its multi-coloured architecture and decorative sculptures, resembling theatre props, create space for everyday life.
The historical core and original layout of the houses have been preserved each with a width of 8–10 m and a depth of around 30 m.
The basic layout of the so-called Lower Town of Lisbon was planned within the limits of three monumental squares: Praça do Comércio, Rossio and Praça da Figueira.
Almeida Fortress is a large military fortification conceived to endure artillery attacks. It has a star-shaped ground-plan with six main bastions, and the citadel is entirely surrounded by a wall.

A regular star-shaped fortress (1691–1731) with the church of St. Anne (1743) in the middle. Placed at the centre of the fortress, the pavilion-style church was designed to stand over an independent tabernacle-altar situated at its centre.

Constructed under Prince Eugene of Savoy as Chairman of the Court Council of War, Slavonski Brod Fortress belongs to the west wing of a large system of Baroque fortress-towns constructed at the Danube node on the border with the Turkish empire.
Built of clay, brick, wood and some stone, the fortress complex was designed to accommodate 4,000 soldiers and 150 cannons.
